new_statements.quote: Most Yaqui words have stress accent. On this point I am in agreement with Johnson (1943) and Dedrick (1946), that is each stem, compound, or idiom said in isolation is characterized by a relatively stable pattern of relative loudness of syllables, though there is perturbation of this stress in running discourse. [...] 4.1. It appears that stress and time are significantly related in my informants' speech. In a great majority of the texts stressed syllables are equally timed relative to each other regardless of the number of unstressed syllables between them. [...] Stress in single words may be governed by a fuller context in the phrase or sentence where stress and time are significantly related.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress accent exists (each stem, compound or idiom has a stable loudness pattern in isolation), but the placement within the word is never stated; the section describes discourse rhythm instead: stressed syllables are isochronous (stress-timed), monosyllables such as Spanish-loan 'lo' are stressed or not according to the stress of neighbouring content words, and in spans of 2-3-syllable words every other syllable may end up stressed. Tone (high/low, rising/falling) is treated separately as intonational/junctural, not lexical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; in discourse 'every other syllable' may be stressed in spans of two- or three-syllable words (§4.3).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress placement varies in running discourse (see texts); 'tone and stress in running discourse are not to be confused' (§5.6).
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Yaqui/Hiaki (yaqu1251) but two varieties: Crumrine 1961, the 2017 pedagogical grammar and Hafner 2018 describe Arizona Hiaki (Pascua/Tucson speakers); Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006 and Dedrick & Casad 1999 describe Sonora Yaqui. Hafner notes the closely related Mayo has a comparable pitch accent system. The file is authored by Florian Hafner alone according to its title page.

new_statements.quote: Most words in Hiaki have a vowel that requires more emphasis. It is usually the first one. However, in some words the emphasis appears on the second vowel, as we have seen for the word havée, 'who', in Lesson 23 above. When it helps to disambiguate between two otherwise similar words, the pitch accent is represented by the accent marker on the vowel that needs to be stressed, as in á, é, í, ó, ú. [...] Stressed vowels in English are often pronounced more loudly. In contrast, in Hiaki, the pitch accented vowels are pronounced more with a higher pitch, but not so much additional loudness.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Most Hiaki words have one prominent vowel, usually the first; a lexically listed minority have it on the second vowel; the prominence is realized as higher pitch rather than loudness and is contrastive (minimal pairs ánia 'world' / anía 'to help', yó'oko 'spotted' / yoóko 'tomorrow', ká'ate 'build' / kaáte 'travel', wíuta 'wave' / wiúta 'tear down').
new_statements.exceptions: Words with accent on the second vowel must be memorized (anía, yoóko, bwichía, vachía, kaáte, wiúta, havée).

new_statements.quote: In that sense, we claim that the unmarked pattern of a lexical item consist of a double aligned trochaic foot requiring strong stress in the first syllable and a high tone in the second syllable. Under affixation, sometimes the double aligned trochaic foot is preserved, but sometimes it is realigned given rise to single aligned iambic feet or to single aligned trochaic feet. Therefore, Yaqui must be classified as a lexical stress-pitch language. [...] In this work we have shown that stress prominence and pitch prominence are both relevant in Yaqui. Stress prominence is basic at morphological level because the prominences readjust according to principles of foot formation. Pitch prominence is important also because it is a distinctive feature in the language

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty. Adds an initial (trochaic) intensity stress as unmarked pattern plus a distinctive pitch tier; disagrees with the pure pitch accent accounts on which cue is the word-level 'stress' (Sonora Yaqui).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two prominence tiers. Intensity/duration stress builds a syllabic trochee from the left edge, so the unmarked word has strong stress on the first syllable; pitch is a separate, lexically distinctive H that in the unmarked ('double aligned trochaic') pattern sits on the second syllable ([S W] + [L H]). Marked patterns: single-aligned iambic (stress and H both final, only nouns, e.g. teput, batat, kiicul, baakot) and single-aligned trochaic (stress and H both initial, e.g. euse, hioste, yeka). The mirror image (double-aligned iambic) is unattested. Under affixation the foot may be realigned. Earlier work (Langendoen & Munguía 1996) had stress on the first or second mora of the stem.
new_statements.exceptions: Single-aligned iambic nouns (stress on the final syllable: teput, batat, kiicul, baakot, uusi, aaki, naamu) and single-aligned trochaic verbs/adjectives (H on first syllable: euse, siari, hioste, yeka); classical minimal pairs káate/kaáte, yóoko/yoóko, téeka/teéka distinguished by pitch.
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Yaqui/Hiaki (yaqu1251) but two varieties: Crumrine 1961, the 2017 pedagogical grammar and Hafner 2018 describe Arizona Hiaki (Pascua/Tucson speakers); Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006 and Dedrick & Casad 1999 describe Sonora Yaqui. Hafner notes the closely related Mayo has a comparable pitch accent system. The file is authored by Florian Hafner alone according to its title page.

new_statements.quote: Hiaki possesses two different types of pitch accents: one is a lexically determined pitch accent and the other is a morphologically determined pitch accent. [...] Hiaki possesses a lexical pitch accent creating minimal pairs such as héeka 'wind' and heéka 'drank'. Demers et al. (1999, p. 41) state that such pairs are true minimal pairs and phonological conditioning can be ruled out as the sole difference between the words is the pitch accent. [...] The minimal pairs above demonstrate that the lexical pitch accent attaches to morae. In káate 'build a house', the pitch accent goes on the first mora whereas it attaches to the second mora in kaáte 'walk'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty. Supplies the standard modern account: lexical pitch accent on first or second mora (Arizona Hiaki), and documents the disagreement among sources on whether prominence is stress or pitch.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hiaki has a lexically specified pitch accent (a high tone) on the first or the second mora of the stem, giving minimal pairs (héeka 'wind' / heéka 'drank', káate / kaáte, yóoko / yoóko, ánia / anía), plus a morphologically determined pitch accent that appears when a long-vowel stem is affixed and the vowel shortens (waawa > wawane, muúmu > mumúta); whether that accent tracks morae or syllables could not be settled by the acoustic and perception experiments. Reviews Fraenkel 1959 as treating prominence as unpredictable stress on the first or second syllable of bisyllables (all monosyllables stressed; trisyllables first+third or second).
new_statements.exceptions: waáte 'people' is not a minimal pair with wáate for the consultant (short first vowel); ánia 'world' had an almost flat pitch in both tokens; the position of the morphological pitch accent under affixation is unresolved.
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Yaqui/Hiaki (yaqu1251) but two varieties: Crumrine 1961, the 2017 pedagogical grammar and Hafner 2018 describe Arizona Hiaki (Pascua/Tucson speakers); Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006 and Dedrick & Casad 1999 describe Sonora Yaqui. Hafner notes the closely related Mayo has a comparable pitch accent system. The file is authored by Florian Hafner alone according to its title page.

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on the nature and default location of Yaqui word prominence, not on its being lexically contrastive. Fraenkel 1959 (as reviewed by Hafner 2018, pp. 11-12) and Langendoen & Munguía 1996 (as reviewed by Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006, p. 1) call it stress, unpredictable, on the first or second syllable/mora of the stem. Demers, Escalante & Jelinek 1999, the 2017 Hiaki pedagogical grammar (pp. 178-179) and Hafner 2018 (pp. 4-5) call it a pitch accent (high pitch, not loudness) on the first or second mora, default first. Martínez Fabián & Munguía Duarte 2006 split the two cues: intensity stress is trochaic and initial in the unmarked word and non-contrastive, while a distinctive high tone sits on the SECOND syllable in that same unmarked pattern ([S W]+[L H]); this puts the default H on the opposite syllable from the pedagogical grammar's 'usually the first' accent (e.g. ánia 'world'), and Hafner (p. 6) measured ánia with an almost flat pitch, so what the accent mark on the first vowel encodes acoustically is unsettled. Crumrine 1961 confirms word-level stress accent exists but gives no placement, describing stress-timed discourse rhythm instead. Dedrick & Casad 1999 (Sonora) and Belloro & Guerrero 2012 could not be opened.
